title: Surgery robot advances precision 10x #surgeryrobot #microsurgery #medicaltech
description: The surgery robot performed precise cuts and suturing on a piece of corn, demonstrating its potential for future medical applications. Controlled by human surgeons through a magnified camera, the robot translates large hand movements into microscale actions, enabling surgeries far smaller than fingertip-width incisions. This advancement allows for operations on tiny blood vessels and nerves, which could revolutionize limb reattachment and nerve repair. The increased precision reduces complications and promotes faster patient recovery, representing a significant leap in minimally invasive surgical technology. Such innovation highlights the impact of robotics in healthcare, promising more delicate, safer procedures that enhance surgical outcomes and patient quality of life. #SurgeryRobot #RoboticSurgery #MinimallyInvasiveSurgery #MedicalRobotics #Microsurgery #LimbReattachment #NerveRepair #SurgicalInnovation #HealthcareTechnology #PrecisionSurgery #SurgicalRobot #MedicalTechnology #FutureOfSurgery #MinimallyInvasiveTech #SurgicalRobotics

top_comments.author: @Dr.WayneManzo
top_comments.text:
This is pretty old technology. What was the old machine called? Da Vinci Robotic System?
If your hospital has one of these it's a very modern hospital but how many surgeons are skilled at using this robot. The next gen design is complete AI automation. To stitch up a piece of corn just show the machine what you want stitch and let the machine do the rest. That is why we invented computerized mechanical system controllers. Or, you can use Opti Mus or
Opti Muse as the Robot Controller that takes instructions from the surgeon. Do the Robots make house calls?
